Keep the Faith, Baby
KEEP thuh FAYTH, BAY-bee
catchphrase (Boomer slang)
The signature farewell of Adam Clayton Powell Jr. (1908–1972), pastor of Harlem’s Abyssinian Baptist Church and U.S. congressman, who used it as a rallying cry, especially in 1967 when the House voted to exclude him amid charges of misusing funds (the Supreme Court later ruled the exclusion unconstitutional, Powell v. McCormack, 1969); his book of sermons was titled Keep the Faith, Baby! (1967). The phrase passed into general use as an upbeat "hang in there." It echoes Paul’s "I have kept the faith" (2Ti 4:7).

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Keep the faith, baby was Adam Clayton Powell’s sign-off, and it became a 1960s and 70s way to say "hang in there, stay strong, don’t give up." The Christian observation: the slogan borrows one of the most important phrases in the New Testament and usually empties it. When Paul wrote, at the end of his life, "I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith" (2Ti 4:7), he did not mean that he had stayed optimistic. He meant he had guarded a definite body of truth — "the faith which was once delivered unto the saints," for which Jude tells believers to "earnestly contend" (Jud 1:3) — and had trusted the Person it reveals, through beatings, shipwreck, and prison. To keep the faith in that sense is to hold the gospel without adding to it or subtracting from it, and to keep trusting Christ until death. "Let us hold fast the profession of our faith without wavering; (for he is faithful that promised;)" (Heb 10:23). "Be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life" (Rev 2:10). Powell himself was a complicated man, a gifted preacher whose public life was marked by scandal, and the slogan’s easy cheerfulness sits beside a hard question every believer must face: what faith am I keeping? A father can say "keep the faith" to his son as a blessing, and mean by it exactly what Paul meant.

Webster 1828 Definition

Adam Clayton Powell Jr.’s 1960s catchphrase (book, 1967) for "hang in there" — a borrowing of Paul’s "I have kept the faith" (2Ti 4:7), which means guarding the faith once delivered (Jud 1:3) and trusting Christ unto death.

expand to see more

KEEP THE FAITH, BABY, catchphrase (1960s; Adam Clayton Powell Jr.) Stay strong; do not give up; remain loyal to the cause. Also simply keep the faith, as a farewell.

Webster (1828) — FAITH, noun [Latin fides, fido, to trust; Gr. to persuade, to draw towards any thing, to conciliate; to believe, to obey. In the Greek Lexicon of Hederic it is said, the primitive signification of the verb is to bind and draw or lead, as signifies a rope or cable. But this remark is a little incorrect. The sense of the verb, from which that of rope and binding is derived, is to strain, to draw, and thus to bind or make fast. A rope or cable is that which makes fast. Heb.] 1. Belief; the assent of the mind to the truth of what is declared by another, resting on his authority and veracity, without other evidence; the judgment that what another states or testifies is the truth. I have strong faith or no faith in the testimony of a witness, or in what a historian narrates. 2. The assent of the mind to the truth of a proposition advanced by another; belief, or probable evidence of any kind. 3.

Decode for families: in the New Testament, the faith is a definite body of truth (Jud 1:3) as well as trust in Christ. Keep both.

Key Scripture

2Ti 4:7 — "I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith:"

Jud 1:3 — "Beloved, when I gave all diligence to write unto you of the common salvation, it was needful for me to write unto you, and exhort you that ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints."

Heb 10:23 — "Let us hold fast the profession of our faith without wavering; (for he is faithful that promised;)"

Rev 2:10 — "Fear none of those things which thou shalt suffer: behold, the devil shall cast some of you into prison, that ye may be tried; and ye shall have tribulation ten days: be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life."

1Co 16:13 — "Watch ye, stand fast in the faith, quit you like men, be strong."

Modern Corruption

The catchphrase turned Paul’s confession into a cheerful "hang in there"; Scripture means by keeping the faith a lifelong guarding of revealed truth and trust in Christ unto death.

expand to see more

Slogans often steal from Scripture, and this one stole a precious phrase. Keep the faith became a way to encourage persistence in any cause — political, personal, athletic — with no particular faith in view. That flattening matches the culture’s view of faith as a feeling of confidence rather than trust in a revealed truth. A man can "keep the faith" in that sense while abandoning every doctrine of the Christian faith.

Paul’s words in 2Ti 4:7 were written from a Roman cell, shortly before his execution. They are a soldier’s report at the end of a campaign: the fight fought, the race run, the deposit guarded. A Christian family can reclaim the phrase by filling it again: the faith of the Apostles’ Creed, the faith of the catechism, the faith in Christ crucified and risen. Keep that faith, and the crown of life (Rev 2:10) is promised.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Latin fides → Old French feid → English faith; Adam Clayton Powell Jr.’s catchphrase (1960s; book 1967) echoing 2Ti 4:7.
